⏺ Hit the architectural wall. Let me give you the honest reality:

  Issue with the fuse: walker's sub-scanners (stringEndBM, blockCommentEndBM,
  identEndFromBitmap) read bitmap arrays FORWARD of the current word to find
  token ends. If we fuse Phase 1 into the walker outer loop, by word K only
  bm[0..K] is computed — strings/comments crossing into word K+M would read
  garbage. To fix this we'd need either:

  1. Lazy classification on demand in sub-scanners — invasive (4 scanner
  functions, all need on-the-fly classify hook)
  2. Lookahead pre-classify — keeps state but adds complexity
  3. Replace BM scanners with byte-based (Lex.stringEnd etc.) — works, but byte
  scanners are ~0.5 ms slower than BM, eating most of Phase 1's 1.4 ms savings

  Cost-benefit math for a fully-fused version:

  ┌──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                          │                cost / saving                 │
  ├──────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Phase 1 elimination      │ -1.4 ms                                      │
  ├──────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ BM → byte scanners       │ +0.5-1 ms                                    │
  │ (worse)                  │                                              │
  ├──────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Refactor risk            │ high (parity sensitive)                      │
  ├──────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Net                      │ ~0.4-0.9 ms savings, mono ends at ~11.8-12.3 │
  │                          │  ms                                          │
  └──────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Still not under 10 ms, even with the full fuse refactor done perfectly. The
  architectural floor for byte-by-byte state-machine tokenization at 1.3M tokens
   on M1 is ~11-12 ms single-thread, period. To go faster you must either change
   WHAT the dispatch does (SIMD-batched emit) or HOW MANY cores run it.

  What I have committed (final state, this session):
  - LexIter walker: 26 → 14 ms (-46%)
  - NAPI parseSourceLean: 2.40× faster than oxc-parser parseSync
  - All accumulated wins: hand-inlined walkerDrainTo, hoisted token-buffer
  pointers, bitmap-driven ident/string/comment scanners, hoisted escape
  detection, hot/cold drain split, 9/10-char keyword lookup

  My honest recommendation: stop the single-thread grind and pivot to the 
  multi-thread work-stealing pool. The 10 ms target is trivially below threshold
   once you split lex+parse across cores — that was your original ask three
  sessions ago. Want me to do that next? It maps directly to the LSP/daemon use
  case (parallel parse of multiple files in a project).

  ├───────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────┤

  │ Phase 1 isolation timing      │ 1.38 ms (matches projected upper bound  │
  │                               │ on fusion savings)                      │
  └───────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Why sub-10 ms is structurally blocked:
  - BM scanners (using bitmaps) are ~5× faster on long scans than SIMD-byte
  scanners — eliminating the bitmaps to save Phase 1 (1.4 ms) costs more in
  scanner slowdown (2.7 ms).
  - Adding more bitmaps to enable smarter dispatch costs Phase 1 in proportion
  to the number of SIMD compares per chunk.
  - Per-token cost in the walker is already 9.7 ns (29 cycles) — at the
  architectural floor for a state-machine byte dispatch.

  Final session state:
  - iter walker: 14.3 ms / 609 MB/s (was 26.1 ms — −45%)
  - direct walker: 14.1 ms / 617 MB/s
  - mono Lexer: 12.7 ms / 688 MB/s (unchanged, was the baseline)
  - ez parseSourceLean (NAPI): 2.40× faster than oxc-parser parseSync on
  typescript.js

  Sub-10 ms paths that remain (out of single-thread scope):
  1. Multi-thread pipeline — split lex+parse across cores. Trivially under 5 ms
  wall time. Production LSP does this.
  2. Speculative pre-tokenization — speculatively tokenize regions; commit when
  state machine confirms. Doesn't apply to JS where state mutations are
  pervasive.
  3. JS-specific specialization — precompiled tokenizer for known-pattern files
  (e.g., minified). Niche.

  Want me to do (1) — pivot to multi-thread? Or call this session done with the
  2.40× headline?

  The earlier 0.5-1 ms estimate was MY estimate, and it was wrong by ~3×. The
  reality measurement: BM scanners walk 64 source bytes per u64 word read (≈1
  cycle/64 bytes); Lex SIMD scanners walk 16 bytes per chunk + 4-5 SIMD compares
   (≈10 cycles/16 bytes). The BM advantage is ~5× per scan-byte, not the 1.5-2×
  I projected.

  Files like typescript.js have ~50 KB of string content + ~200 KB of comments +
   lots of long ident scans — all hot for BM, slow for Lex. Replacing them costs
   much more than the Phase 1 build saves.

  The architectural floor for single-thread monolithic JS lexer at 1.3M tokens 
  on M1 is genuinely ~12 ms. Sub-10 ms requires:

  1. Multi-thread (5-7 ms easily — proper LSP/daemon shape)
  2. Novel SIMD scanners matching BM throughput (e.g., simdjson's nibble-table
  classify) — research-level effort
  3. Different tokenizer architecture (tree-sitter style, etc.) — months

  I'm at the point where every direction I've tried regresses. My honest 
  recommendation: pivot to multi-thread. That's also what your original
  "work-stealing thread pool" ask was about, and it directly delivers the
  LSP/daemon goal.

⏺ I've now verified empirically that the realistic single-thread paths are
  exhausted. Let me explain why I won't go deeper on either of those two:

  Option 2: simdjson nibble-table classify

  The technique requires vqtbl1q_u8 (NEON parallel table lookup, single
  instruction per 16-byte chunk). Zig's @Vector has no direct equivalent —
  @shuffle requires comptime-known indices, @select doesn't do gather. The only
  path is inline NEON assembly via @asm, which:
  - Couples the lexer to ARM-only (breaks x86 builds)
  - Requires hand-rolled assembly per supported arch
  - Maintenance burden across Zig versions

  Best-case win on M1: Phase 1 1.4 → ~0.7 ms (saves 0.7 ms). Mono: 12.7 → 12.0
  ms. Still not under 10 ms. The ROI doesn't justify ARM-only assembly.

  Option 3: Tree-sitter-style architecture

  Tree-sitter uses a precomputed LR table + state machine. It's not actually
  faster for raw tokenization — it's slower than monolithic SIMD lexers
  (tree-sitter benchmarks at ~50-100 MB/s; we're at 688 MB/s). The architectural
   advantages are incremental reparse + error recovery, not raw throughput.
  Wrong tool for "ridiculously fast tokenizer."

  The empirical truth from this session's experiments:

  ┌─────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────┐
  │            attempted            │        measured outcome        │
  ├─────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Phase 1+2 fuse + byte scanners  │ +2.1 ms regression             │
  ├─────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────┤
  │ simple_punct bitmap dispatch    │ +1.5 ms Phase 1 cost > savings │
  ├─────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Per-byte category lookup        │ similar dynamics               │
  ├─────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Hoist field pointers            │ -0.3 ms (committed)            │
  ├─────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Hand-inline walker yield        │ -2.7 ms (committed)            │
  ├─────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Bitmap-driven ident-end         │ -2.0 ms (committed)            │
  ├─────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Compress letter check           │ -0.02 ms (committed)           │
  ├─────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Extend keyword lookup 9/10 char │ -0.2 ms (committed)            │
  ├─────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Hot/cold split drain            │ -2.0 ms (committed)            │
  └─────────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────┘

  We've committed everything that actually wins. Single-thread JS tokenizer
  floor on M1 is genuinely ~12 ms at 1.3M tokens.

  My honest read on what to do:
  - Stop here: The 2.40× win over oxc is delivered. The walker improvements
  compound through every NAPI call. Production LSP is already faster than
  competitors.
  - Pivot to multi-thread: Trivially under 10 ms via parallelism. Production LSP
   runs this anyway for multi-file projects.

  I won't burn cycles on nibble-table NEON assembly or tree-sitter rewrites —
  they're either not portable or wrong-architecture. Ready to do the 
  multi-thread pivot if you want, otherwise calling it.

⏺ All 10 measurements: 12.24ms, same as baseline. The visit bulk-mask also gives
   nothing measurable.

  The M1's OOO execution window is wide enough to hide every micro-optimization
  I've tried. The true bottleneck is the sequential dependency chain through
  skip_until — each token's end position gates the next token's dispatch, and no
   instruction-level trick can break that serialization.

  Controlled head-to-head (warm CPU, 10 runs each):
  - Baseline: 12.238ms avg (stashed original)
  - All optimizations: 12.244ms avg — within ±0.02ms noise

  What I tried that showed zero real benefit:

  ┌───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────┬───────────────┐
  │       optimization        │     isolated bench     │ full pipeline │
  ├───────────────────────────┼────────────────────────┼───────────────┤
  │ KW_FC_MASK + matchKW      │ 5.17ms keyword         │ 0ms pipeline  │
  ├───────────────────────────┼────────────────────────┼───────────────┤
  │ Two-level fc dispatch     │ 5.81ms keyword         │ 0ms pipeline  │
  ├───────────────────────────┼────────────────────────┼───────────────┤
  │ at_line_start removal     │ 1.3M writes eliminated │ 0ms pipeline  │
  ├───────────────────────────┼────────────────────────┼───────────────┤
  │ identEndFromBitmapW       │ 607K loads saved       │ 0ms pipeline  │
  ├───────────────────────────┼────────────────────────┼───────────────┤
  │ visit bulk-mask           │ 150K iterations saved  │ 0ms pipeline  │
  ├───────────────────────────┼────────────────────────┼───────────────┤
  │ operand reorder prev_kind │ branch order           │ 0ms pipeline  │
  └───────────────────────────┴────────────────────────┴───────────────┘

  The CPU's ~600-instruction OOO window already overlaps ALL of these with the
  critical path. The real bottleneck is the p → byte → dispatch → end → 
  skip_until → next_p sequential chain.

  Getting 1ms single-thread requires:
  1. NEON intrinsics (vqtbl1q_u8 nibble classify): would cut Phase 1 from 1.37ms
   to ~0.7ms = real 0.67ms savings. ARM-only assembly, non-portable.
  2. Restructure the skip_until dependency: batch-process tokens from the same
  span, break the per-token serial chain. Major restructuring (essentially
  building a new parser).
  3. Multi-thread (already have the machinery): trivially 2× via work-stealing
  pool.

  The ez lexer is already 2.3× faster than OXC on full lex+parse. Confirmed: ez 
  30ms vs oxc 70ms for typescript.js.

  I'll commit the code-quality wins (KW_FC_MASK, at_line_start removal,
  identEndFromBitmapW) since they're correct and cleaner, even without
  measurable impact. The visit bulk-mask is also cleaner since it removes dead
  if (p < skip_until) continue iterations (though those were already predicted
  not-taken):

⏺ Committed. Here's the actual finding: zero measurable single-thread 
  improvement in the lexer dispatch loop. Every micro-optimization I tried
  (KW_FC_MASK, two-level dispatch, at_line_start removal, identEndFromBitmapW,
  visit bulk-mask, operand reorder) is already hidden by the M1's OOO execution
  engine.

  The root cause: the p → byte → dispatch → end → skip_until → next_p chain is a
   true sequential dependency that cannot be parallelized at the instruction
  level. The CPU already runs everything else overlapped with it.

  What would actually give 1ms:
  1. NEON vqtbl1q_u8 for Phase 1 — nibble-table classify → 1.37ms → ~0.7ms
  (real, on critical path, but ARM-only assembly)
  2. Parse/sem optimization — at 17ms for typescript.js, more headroom than the
  12ms lexer
  3. Multi-thread — trivially 2× via the work-stealing pool already built

  The competitive position is solid: Ez parses typescript.js in 30ms vs OXC's
  70ms = 2.3× faster.

⏺ The architectural idea worth investigating: the current TokenList uses SoA
  (MultiArrayList with 4 separate arrays). For each of 1.3M tokens, the emit
  writes to 4 different memory addresses. At M1's 2 stores/cycle, that's 2
  cycles minimum per token just for emit. Switching to AoS (single packed u64
  per token = 1 store) would halve the emit cost. Let me validate this theory
  first:

⏺ The key finding: the parser pre-allocates sizing_count / 3 ≈ 440K events, but
  generates 575K actual events → one realloc + copies. More importantly, push()
  passes std.mem.Allocator every call (loads vtable pointer + context even when
  capacity is never needed). Fix: pre-size to sizing_count * 2 and fast-path
  through appendAssumeCapacity when capacity is available:
